en: In the beginning, indeed, this was the Self alone; there was nothing else whatsoever blinking. He thought: "Shall I now create the worlds? (AitU 1.1.1)
He created these worlds: Ambhas, Marīcis, Mara, and Āpas.
Ambhas is that which is beyond the sky;
the sky is its support.
The intermediate space is the rays;
the earth is the dust;
those that are below are the waters.
He reflected: "These worlds now exist;
let me create guardians of the worlds.
From the waters alone, he drew forth a person and gave him form.
He brooded over it;
from it, thus brooded upon, the mouth was split open like an eggshell,
and from the mouth, speech emerged.
From speech, fire was produced;
the two nostrils were pierced open;
from the nostrils, breath was produced.
From the vital breath (prāṇa) came the wind (vāyu); the two eyes were split open;
from the two eyes came sight (cakṣus).
From the eye, the sun [was produced];
the two ears were split open;
from the ears, hearing [arose].
From the ear, the directions emerged;
the skin was split open;
from the skin, the body hairs emerged.
From the body hairs came the plants and trees;
the heart burst forth;
from the heart came the mind.
From the mind, the moon was produced;
the navel burst forth;
from the navel, the downward breath (apāna) arose.
From the downward breath, death was produced;
the male organ burst forth;
from the male organ, semen was produced.
From semen, water.
These deities, having been created, fell into this great ocean;
he afflicted them with hunger and thirst. They said to him, "Find for us a dwelling place."
"Upon what, being established, shall we bestow food?"—thus [they asked]. AitUp 1.2.1.
He brought a cow for them;
they said, "This one is certainly not enough for us.
He brought a horse for them.
They said, "Truly, this one is not sufficient for us. (AitU 1.2.2)
From them he brought forth a man.
They said, "Ah, what a well-made thing!
Man, indeed, is the well-made thing.
He said to them, "Enter according to your respective abodes. (AitU 1.2.3)
Agni, having become speech, entered the mouth;
Vāyu, having become breath, entered the nostrils;
Āditya, having become sight, entered the eyes.
The quarters, having become the sense of hearing, entered the ears;
the herbs and trees, having become the body hairs, entered the skin;
the moon, having become the mind, entered the heart.
Death, having become the *apāna* breath, entered the navel;
the waters, having become semen, entered the penis.
Hunger and thirst said to him, "Take us into account.
He replied, "I shall assign you a share among these very deities; I shall make you partners in them.
Therefore, for whichever deity an oblation is taken, hunger and thirst become partners in it.
He reflected: "Now here are these worlds and the guardians of the worlds;
let me create food for them. (AitUp 1.3.1)
He brooded upon the waters.
From those waters, thus brooded upon, a form was born.
That form which was born is indeed food. (AitU 1.3.2)
Once it was created, it sought to flee away;
he tried to seize it with speech,
but he was not able to grasp it with speech.
If he had grasped it by means of speech alone, he would have been satisfied with food merely after pronouncing it.
He sought to grasp it with the vital breath (prāṇa).
He was not able to grasp it with the vital breath.
Had he grasped it with the vital breath, one would have swallowed food merely by breathing upon it.
He sought to grasp it with the eye;
he was not able to grasp it with the eye. Had he been able to grasp it with the eye, one would have been satisfied merely by seeing food. (AitU 1.3.5)
He desired to grasp it with the ear. He was not able to grasp it with the ear.
Had he grasped it with the ear, one would have been satisfied by merely hearing the food. (AitU 1.3.6)
He sought to grasp it with the skin;
he was not able to grasp it with the skin.
Had he grasped it with the skin, he would have been satisfied by merely touching food.
He desired to grasp it with the mind. He was not able to grasp it with the mind. Had he grasped it with the mind, one would have attained food merely by thinking of it. (AitU 1.3.8)
He sought to grasp it with his penis;
he was not able to grasp it with his penis.
Had he grasped it with his penis, he would have become insatiable for food even after discharging it. (AitU 1.3.9)
He sought to grasp it with the out-breath; he swallowed it. This wind is that seizer of food.
Vāyu, indeed, is life-breath.
He reflected: "How indeed might this exist without me? He reflected: "By which way shall I enter?
He reflected: "Whether it be what is articulated by speech, or what is breathed forth by breath, or what is seen by the eye, or what is heard by the ear..."
"If it has been heard by the ear, or touched by the skin, or meditated upon by the mind, or inhaled by the breath, or emitted by the organ of generation—then who am I? (AitU 1.3.11)
He split open this very suture and entered through that door;
that is the door named Vidṛti,
and that is the Nāndana grove.
He has three abodes and three states of sleep: "This is an abode, this is an abode, this is an abode. (AitU 1.3.12)
Once born, he looked upon all beings, thinking, "What else here could one possibly speak of?
He beheld this very Person as the most pervasive Brahman, [thinking], "I have seen this. 3 // AitUp_1,3.13 //
Therefore, his name is Idandra. Indeed, his name is Idandra;
though he is Idandra, they call him Indra by an indirect name.
For the gods, as it were, delight in what is out of sight; for the gods, as it were, delight in what is out of sight.
Verily, this embryo first exists within a man as this semen. Having been produced from the vital energy of all his limbs, he bears that self within his own self.
When he pours it into a woman, then he brings it forth.
That is his first birth. (AitUp 2.1)
It becomes the very self of that woman, just like her own limb;
therefore, it does not harm her.
She, in turn, contemplates this Self of his as having entered into her here. (AitU 2.2)
She becomes the one who brings it forth and that which is to be brought forth;
she, the woman, bears that embryo,
and he, at the very beginning, brings the boy into being prior to birth.
When he contemplates the boy at the beginning of his birth, he thereby contemplates his own self for the continuity of these worlds;
for thus are these worlds continuous.
That is his second birth. (AitUp 2.3)
Thus, this self of his is assigned to meritorious deeds;
then his other self, having accomplished its purpose and reached the end of its lifespan, departs.
As soon as he departs from here, he is born again.
That is his third birth. (AitUp 2.4)
This was said by the Seer: "While still in the womb, I indeed knew all these births of the gods;
a hundred iron fortresses protected me, and then, like a hawk, I flew forth with speed.
Thus it is said.
While still lying within the womb, Vāmadeva spoke thus. (AitU 2.5)
Knowing this, he, having ascended upwards after the dissolution of this body, having attained all desires in that heavenly world, became immortal—he became immortal. (AitUp 2.6)
"Who is this whom we venerate as the Self?
Which one is that Self?"

That by which one sees, or that by which one hears, or that by which one smells odors, or that by which one articulates speech, or that by which one discerns what is sweet and what is not sweet. (AitU 3.1)

That which is this heart and this mind— consciousness, comprehension, discernment, wisdom, intelligence, vision, steadfastness, thought, reflection, impetus, memory, volition, purpose, life-force, desire, and will— all these are indeed names for wisdom. (Aitareya Upaniṣad 3.2)
This is Brahmā;
this is Indra;
this is Prajāpati.
All these are the gods;

and these five great elements—earth, wind, space, water, and light—as well as these others, like small mixed seeds, some one way and some another: those born from eggs, those born from wombs, those born from sweat, and those born from sprouts, such as horses and cattle.
Men, elephants, whatever living beings there are— whether moving or flying, or that which is stationary—
all that has wisdom as its eye; all is established in wisdom.
The world has wisdom as its eye;
wisdom is its foundation;
Brahman is knowledge. (Aitareya Upaniṣad 3.3)
Having departed from this world by means of this wise self, he attained all desires in that heavenly world and became immortal—he became immortal. AitUp 3.4.
